q-65249:
First, we factor the denominator:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta }=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}
$$

Next, we use the Pythagorean identity to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, and then we simplify the resulting expression as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta }=\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

q-72712:
First, we factor $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ from the first two terms:

$$
\frac{{sin}^{3}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x+1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)+1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}
$$

Next, we use the Pythagorean identity to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, and then we simplify the resulting expression as much as possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)+1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that:

$$
\frac{{sin}^{3}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x+1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x
$$

q-119770:
We put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1} \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{1(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)} \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify using the Pythagorean identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x} & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x=1.
$$

q-43298:
First, we expand the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}}+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

We put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1}+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify using the Pythagorean identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡t(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t})=\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

q-1708:
Recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$

Applying the sum formula for sine with $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $y=\frac{\pi }{6}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-65430:
Recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$

Applying the difference formula for sine with $x=\frac{7\pi }{6}$ and $y=\frac{\pi }{4}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{11\pi }{12}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6}-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-141275:
Recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

Applying the difference formula for sine with $u=x$ and $v={120}^{∘},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-{120}^{∘}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡{120}^{∘}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡{120}^{∘} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-65438:
Recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

Applying the difference formula for sine with $u=x$ and $v={45}^{∘},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-{45}^{∘}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡{45}^{∘}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

q-65437:
Recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

Applying the sum formula for sine with $u=x$ and $v=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

q-141284:
Recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

Applying the difference formula for sine with $u=x$ and $v=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (1) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-109000:
The velocity is the derivative of the position function $x(t)$ with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{2t({t}^{2}+1)-{t}^{2}(2t)}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2{t}^{3}+2t-2{t}^{3}}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2t}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

q-19299:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{e}^{-t}+3{t}^{2}-2t+1) \\  & =-4{e}^{-t}+6t-2\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the velocity at $t=2,$ we substitute $t=2$ into the velocity function above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =-4{e}^{-2}+6\cdot 2-2 \\  & =-4{e}^{-2}+10 \\  & =9.458\,658… \\  & ≈9.46\end{aligned}
$$

q-109012:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{t}) \\  & =-\frac{3}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=3,$ the velocity is

$$
v(3)=-\frac{3}{{3}^{2}}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the speed is $|-\frac{1}{3}|=\frac{1}{3}\,\text{miles/h}.$

q-113502:
Let $u=2-5x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 18(2-5x)^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int 18{u}^{5}\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})\text{d}u \\  & =18\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})\int {u}^{5}\cdot \,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{18}{5}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{18}{5}\cdot \frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}{u}^{6}+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}(2-5x)^{6}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{3}{5}(2-5x)^{6}+C] & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{3}{5}(2-5x)^{6}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =-\frac{18}{5}(2-5x)^{5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2-5x)+0 \\  & =-\frac{18}{5}(2-5x)^{5}\cdot (-5) \\  & =18(2-5x)^{5}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

q-72424:
Let $u=7-2x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 16(7-2x)^{7}\,\text{d}x & =\int 16{u}^{7}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\int {u}^{7}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\int {u}^{7}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-8\cdot \frac{{u}^{8}}{8}+C \\  & =-{u}^{8}+C \\  & =-(7-2x)^{8}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-(7-2x)^{8}+C] & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(7-2x)^{8}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =-8(7-2x)^{7}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(7-2x)+0 \\  & =-8(7-2x)^{7}\cdot (-2) \\  & =16(7-2x)^{7}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

q-113509:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (x-2)^{-3}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-2.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (x-2)^{-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int {u}^{-3}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {u}^{-2}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2(x-2)^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{1}{2(x-2)^{2}}+C] & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{1}{2(x-2)^{2}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(x-2)^{-2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2)\cdot (x-2)^{-3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x-2)+0 \\  & =1\cdot \frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
